items.title: sanstun: A sans-IO, parallel-friendly WireGuard implementation in Rust
items.author: wh33zle
items.content:
Today, we are announcing : a sans-IO Rust implementation of the WireGuard® state machine, optimized for ease of use, security and performance through a parallel-friendly and idiomatic API.

sans-IO is the idea that you design your system such that IO and side-effects are cleanly separated from the state and "business logic". The IO in sans-IO doesn't just mean file or network IO. It also includes things like time and randomness!

Due to their lack of side-effects, sans-IO components compose very well and are relatively easy to test. The design also avoids problems like function coloring and plays well with Rust's ownership rules.

The code examples and references in this post are in Rust but sans-IO isn't Rust-specific at all. Its patterns and ideas can be applied in any language. For a more in-depth explanation, our sans-IO post is a good place to start.

When we first built Firezone, we reached for as our WireGuard implementation. more or less did what we wanted, but over time, we found ourselves patching our fork over and over with bug fixes as well as API additions. The goal was to allow these patches to still be upstreamed, so we always kept the existing API working the way it was.

What we found was that retaining 100% API compatibility with upstream was increasingly difficult as our product requirements evolved. One of the first big changes we made to was to make it fully sans-IO with regard to time handling (firezone/boringtun#5). This meant adding new APIs for everything with a suffix that would take an . sans-IO time handling is very important if you want to accurately simulate an entire system. See this blog post to learn more about how we do that.

Another thing we feature-flagged was internal buffering. At first, it seems convenient that establishes a session automatically if you don't have one yet (or anymore) and you are trying to send a packet. Internal buffering, however, comes with several problems:

  1. At some point, the buffer needs to be drained. solves this by requiring you to call with a zero-length datagram. Rather unintuitive.
  2. It incurs additional allocations (at least in the way it was implemented in ).
  3. Buffer sizes should be configurable / tunable.

All of these problems point at the same solution: Just don't buffer in the library. It simplifies the interface and the implementation on both sides.

The full list of patches and fixes is pretty long. Even excluding dependency bumps, that is more than 70 PRs. Several of them are fixes for edge-cases we discovered. Others add new APIs or make certain aspects configurable.

After more than 2 years of using and patching , we had a pretty good idea of what the overall API of a userspace WireGuard implementation should be. Now it exists as .

The core building blocks of the sans-IO API are now:

  • Handling inbound packets:
    • Tunnel::handle_handshake_initiation
    • Tunnel::handle_handshake_response
    • Tunnel::handle_cookie_reply
    • Tunnel::begin_decapsulate & Tunnel::commit_decapsulate
  • Handling outbound packets: Tunnel::begin_encapsulate
  • Handling timer updates: &
  • Handling events:

Without internal buffering, there is no API contract that requires you to call certain APIs in a loop, which fits much better into the overall sans-IO model. To send a packet, you call Tunnel::begin_encapsulate. It is up to you to buffer the packet if you don't have a session yet. Creating a new session means sending a handshake. You can initiate a new handshake at any point with Tunnel::initiate_handshake.

The design of these APIs is very deliberate and will make more sense if we quickly recap the WireGuard protocol.

WireGuard's message format supports 4 types of messages: handshake init, handshake response, cookie reply and encrypted data.

Every WireGuard session starts with a Diffie-Hellman key exchange which is a moderately expensive operation. WireGuard's design ensures that exposing an endpoint doesn't open up a DoS opportunity.

Anyone who knows the endpoint's public key can easily create bogus handshake initiations and forge the source IP of the incoming UDP packet. The receiving WireGuard implementation has to run its half of the DH operations before it can tell that the supplied handshake data is bogus. But at that point, the CPU resources have already been spent. Send enough handshake initiations and the receiving end will spend all its CPU cycles on handling irrelevant handshakes.

To prevent this, WireGuard specifies a cookie mechanism that forces the remote to prove ownership of its claimed source IP, which in turn allows rate-limiting handshakes per source IP.

These rate limits apply to an entire WireGuard interface and not just to a single tunnel.

Once a handshake has been completed, both peers can exchange encrypted data packets with a symmetric cipher. As part of the handshake, the peers also exchange their locally-chosen session indices. These indices enable de-multiplexing of tunnels as well as multiple sessions within a tunnel.

If you are working in a language like Rust, chances are you enjoy using types. And using types well means enforcing invariants at compile-time such that you can't even ship a certain bug in the first place. For example, forgetting to apply the rate limiter to a message would be pretty bad because it doesn't show up under normal operation. Similarly, routing an incoming packet to the wrong tunnel is something that will only show up in production.

A good API design makes it impossible to build things that are broken and also guides you along in understanding how the protocol works.

A WireGuard interface is identified by a single key and a tunnel is a connection between two interfaces. Any time we want to send a packet, we therefore need to specify which tunnel it should be sent on and when we receive a packet, we need to figure out which tunnel it belongs to.

In , these concepts directly map to the and types. All inbound packets go through . That is the only public API that parses a raw datagram. It parses the packet, applies rate limits and hands you back a with one enum variant per WireGuard message type, or a cookie reply to send back if the interface is under load. These then map directly to the corresponding functions on a : Tunnel::handle_handshake_initiation, etc. Handshake initiations are routed by the initiator's static public key. All other messages expose they should be dispatched to, identified by a .

Under the hood, does a lot of things for you here. It parses the tunnel index and extracts the upper 24 bits, it applies rate limits, generates cookie replies and validates handshake messages.

Crucially, the constructors for types like are all crate-private. Even though exposes a public handle_handshake_initiation function, the only way to call that is by going through first to obtain such a type. And protects your application by applying the rate limiter, all without you having to think about it.

One of the best features of is its parallel-friendly API for encrypting and decrypting packets.

On a protocol level, WireGuard doesn't share any state between tunnels. Therefore, parallelizing a WireGuard implementation across peers is very easy.

But what about parallelizing work within a single tunnel? WireGuard operates on layer 3, and thus a single session with another peer carries the traffic of many individual network flows. Even if we handle tunnels to different peers on different threads, all network flows (i.e., unique 5-tuples) toward the same host or subnet will be processed sequentially, effectively bounded by how fast the CPU is at ChaCha20-Poly1305, WireGuard's cipher for data packets. To protect against replay by malicious on-path observers, WireGuard data packets have a monotonically increasing packet counter. This counter is scoped to a single session and therefore would require synchronization if we were to access this state from multiple threads simultaneously.

To avoid this, separates the bookkeeping from the actual encryption and decryption. Calling Tunnel::begin_encapsulate doesn't in fact encrypt anything. It checks for the current session, reserves a packet counter, advances timer state and then hands you a :

 {
    <>(, plaintext: &[], dst: & []) <DataMessage<>, Error> {
        
    }
}

implements and can thus be transferred to another thread to perform the bulk of the work. Running in the repository showcases the effect of this split:

data_path/64B/begin_encapsulate
                        time:   [20.785 ns 20.828 ns 20.869 ns]
data_path/64B/encrypt   time:   [226.15 ns 226.22 ns 226.29 ns]
data_path/64B/begin_decapsulate
                        time:   [37.600 ns 37.675 ns 37.744 ns]
data_path/64B/decrypt   time:   [205.78 ns 205.83 ns 205.87 ns]
data_path/64B/commit_decapsulate
                        time:   [17.486 ns 17.529 ns 17.575 ns]

data_path/1280B/begin_encapsulate
                        time:   [20.785 ns 20.828 ns 20.869 ns]
data_path/1280B/encrypt time:   [933.49 ns 933.54 ns 933.59 ns]
data_path/1280B/begin_decapsulate
                        time:   [37.606 ns 37.681 ns 37.751 ns]
data_path/1280B/decrypt time:   [914.81 ns 914.89 ns 914.97 ns]
data_path/1280B/commit_decapsulate
                        time:   [17.657 ns 17.707 ns 17.764 ns]

As expected, the bookkeeping parts (, and ) do not scale with packet size. What does scale with packet size are the and functions. At a packet size of 1280 bytes, the bookkeeping part of encrypting a new packet is only 2%. If we move the actual encryption to another thread, this hints at a potential speedup of more than 45x!

An effective speedup of 45x is hard to achieve in practice because it ignores the cost of passing to another thread and assumes no other overhead is introduced. Nevertheless, being able to offload the crypto to worker threads allows for some great throughput improvements.

Being a sans-IO library, doesn't concern itself with how exactly you want to parallelize your crypto. If you want to keep it simple, you can also just call and inline and not bother with parallelization at all.

The key thing we wanted to achieve with 's API design was to enable parallel crypto while keeping everything around single-threaded. This lets the internal rate limiter work without locks or atomic counters and take advantage of Rust's borrow checker, all while combining state from multiple tunnels.

With , our fork at is now deprecated. If you are building on top of WireGuard, whether that's a VPN, a mesh network or something else entirely, we hope makes your life a little easier. It is available on crates.io.

items.title: AO3 Down for Maintenance
items.author: idlewords
items.content:
Earlier today, we detected evidence of a security incident on AO3. We are still in the early stages of response to this security incident and determining its scope. AO3 will remain down while we continue investigating and addressing what has been found so far. However, we want to make some things clear:

First, no AO3 data has been deleted. All your works, bookmarks, kudos, etc., are safe.

Second, while we currently don't believe that the user database was stolen, we are also unable to rule it out. The AO3 database contains account information that may include your username, email address, IP address, and a hashed version of your password.

We use industry-standard techniques for storing passwords in a scrambled form that cannot easily be reversed. Even so, no hashing method can fully protect a weak or reused password from being cracked. As a precaution, we recommend that you change your passwords on any other sites where you use the same password as on AO3.

AO3 does not collect real names, so none could be exposed. Additionally, our donor information is held in an entirely separate system and is never linked to AO3, so that data has also not been exposed.

We will update everyone as our investigation continues; we may be unable to respond to individual inquiries from users. Please keep an eye on our official outlets for updates. Our next update will be posted when we have further information available.

Our current expectation is that AO3 will be down for a minimum of two weeks; however, it could take up to four weeks. During that time, we may be able to bring the site back up in a degraded state, meaning that not all features will be available and/or the site may be read-only. If we are able to do that, please be aware that we might have to bring the site back down unexpectedly as part of our recovery efforts. We will keep you in the loop for any developments.

items.content: In 1863, Jules Verne did something he would almost never do again. He looked not toward an undiscovered island, the bottom of the sea, the interior of the Earth or the far side of the Moon, but directly into the future. He imagined Paris almost a century ahead, in the year 1960, and asked what sort of civilization the nineteenth century might become if its faith in science, machinery, commerce and efficiency were allowed to run to its logical conclusion. The result was Paris in the Twentieth Century, a book so unlike the Verne we came to know that his publisher, Pierre-Jules Hetzel, refused to publish it. items.title: The oldest ice disappears and the Stone Age emerges from it
items.author: dxs
items.content:
For exactly 20 years, archaeologists working with Secrets of the Ice have been recovering and preserving artefacts emerging from the ice in the mountains of Innlandet, eastern Norway.

Until now, most of the objects have been up to 2,000 years old. Many date from the Viking Age.

But the ancient ice is now beginning to melt.

And within this oldest ice lie the oldest finds: large quantities of arrow shafts and arrowheads from the Bronze Age and the Stone Age.

One of the oldest finds from this year's first field expedition is an arrow with an arrowhead and shaft made of slate.

By comparing it with previously discovered arrows, archaeologists estimate that it is between 5,000 and 6,000 years old.

The preservation conditions in the ice have meant that organic material, such as wood, leather, and textiles, have also survived.

“This year, we found 48 prehistoric arrows. That's a lot,” Espen Finstad, who leads Secrets of the Ice, tells Science Norway.

He explains that, with these latest discoveries, more than 100 arrowheads and arrow shafts have now been recovered from a single ice patch over the years.

The oldest arrowheads are made from slate, freshwater mussel shells, and bone. More recent arrowheads are made from iron and are 'only' between 1,000 and 1,500 years old.

But this year’s fieldwork carries an added sense of gravity.

Finstad explains that the work of recovering archaeological artefacts from the ice has always carried a certain duality.

“It’s fun going around looking for things. It’s exciting, and finding something is just really cool," he says.

Yet behind the excitement lies the reality of climate change. Finstad points to the recent landslide in Nepal and the glacier collapse in Jotunheimen.

“We have always acknowledged this contradiction and the reality behind our work. But this is the first time it has truly affected us on an emotional level,” Finstad says, adding:

“This year, there was a much deeper sense of seriousness and sadness. Only patches of ice remain where we once had large ice patches. It's brutal. And this year, that reality struck us more forcefully than ever before."

Finstad and his colleagues estimate that most of the ice patches containing archaeological artefacts will have disappeared within the next 20 years.

“There has been ice here for 6,000–7,000 years. Nature has been warning us and sending signals for many years. But now it's giving up. Now it is simply going to melt,” says the glacial archaeologist.

'For thousands of years, ancient ice has safely preserved unique objects from the past. Now that ice is disappearing,' the archaeologists write in a press release about the finds. 'We have been at the edge of the ice. We have seen it happening. And we are witnesses to a rapidly changing archaeological landscape.'

Finstad and his colleagues are planning more fieldwork in the coming weeks, weather permitting.

So far, they have secured finds in the Kvittingskjølen mountain area of Jotunheimen, specifically at Langfonne, Storefonne, and Hanklefonne.

Several of the finds are already on display at the Norwegian Mountain Centre in Lom, just a few days after they were discovered.

items.title: The federated code forge
items.author: zlliang
items.content:
For most of the past two decades, the code forge has been where projects live: where code is hosted, where changes are reviewed, and where contributors find each other. Forges offered convenience in exchange for centralisation.

But the centralised forge is crumbling. Relying on someone else for uptime, for features, and to be a good steward of your code hasn’t played out well. What stood the test of time is email: Git to move the code, and email — an open protocol — to talk about it. At the cost of user experience, however.

Tangled aims to give you the best of both: the longevity of an open protocol, with the convenience and polish of a proper forge.

It’s the first truly federated code forge — you can host code on your own servers and still collaborate seamlessly with others. Our approach is pragmatic: self-host just the parts you want, like Git hosting or CI runners, or all of it, including the API server and UI. Whatever you choose, you can still talk to everyone else.

Owning your infrastructure also means you can hack on, extend and customise your forge as you see fit. Because Tangled is built on the AT Protocol, you can build your own extensions, subscribe to the firehose, or even write entirely custom knots, like this one that runs on Cloudflare Workers and uses their Artifacts product for git storage. Or an entirely custom spindle such as mitchellh.com/tack. Go even further and host our ultralight API server and build your own custom forge.

Agents have made building such hyper-personalized software trivial, and especially so when software is designed with hackability in mind from the get-go. Tangled is incredibly agentfriendly.

The future of software engineering may be a moving target, but our bets on open protocols and developer agency give us the agility to move with it, and to become .

The obvious big one: with this release, Tangled has a whole new look. We’ve redone the UI on top of our new architecture (described further below), in Svelte. Things should now be quicker, visually consistent and prettier! The keen eyed of you might’ve also spotted that we’ve swapped out Inter for Timeless Sans.

Until now, Tangled’s web UI and backend were a single Go monolith called the . The appview service handled AT Protocol indexing, caching, off-protocol data and UI rendering using + htmx. It ran on a single SQLite database on one medium-sized server in Sweden.

This was great as long as you were ~50–100 ms away from Sweden, but most of our users aren’t! We rearchitected: we built a new standalone frontend app in Svelte, deployed at the edge. It is populated by our new diskless, entirely in-memory indexer service written in Rust: bobbin. Bobbins are deployed globally in over 11+ regions, ensuring users around the world get the best API and UI performance.

The astute reader might’ve noticed: bobbin is purely read-only and only deals with AT Protocol data. What of the rest? That functionality (and more) has been delegated to a new set of supporting services.

The new data model and repo-owned data

First, the data model itself: we have a new set of lexicons, and everything now lives under , replacing the old records.

Knot2 is our aptly named, second implementation of the knot server, this time rewritten in Rust. Knot2 bakes a fully custom Git server, and also bundles in an SSH server in the same binary.

With knot2, we’ve also changed where some of that data lives. Issues, pull requests, comments, reactions and labels are now stored on the knot, right next to the code, as collaborative objects (COBs). A COB is just a chain of Git objects in the repo itself. Collaborators, knot members and the blocklist are also stored the same way.

In that sense, knots now behave a lot like a PDS: they hold signed records, full history included, for everything that belongs to a repo and much like a PDS, these records are synced via the standard AT Protocol firehose.

But why? A project’s issues and pull requests are as much a part of it as its code, so they should live with it, wherever you choose to host it. This gives your project maximum portability.

If the knot writes your issues and comments, what stops it from putting words in your mouth? Attestations. Every time you create or edit a record on a knot, the web app also writes an org.tangled.graph.attestation record to your own PDS, pointing at that exact version of the record and the COB change behind it. Two-way verification!

Organization accounts are here! An Organization on Tangled is a real AT Protocol account, with its own DID and handle, hosted on a Tranquil PDS instance. They’re passwordless, delegated accounts: you create one from the New Organization page, and you get with yourself as its owner. Owners can invite members, and anyone in the Organization can act as it when creating or forking repositories. Like any other account, you can swap the handle out for a domain you own. If you’ve been running a regular account as a stand-in “org”, hang tight — we’re working on a way to move those over. Read more in the docs.

Our PR flow has been overhauled. The new flow gives everyone, regardless of whether you use Jujutsu or just vanilla Git, the ability to submit and review stacked PRs. If you’re using Git, you now get the ability to interdiff between versions (previously called rounds). JJ users get to interdiff between individual changes as well.

This isn’t all. We’re staggering this launch across the next few weeks. Up next are private repos, a CLI, SDKs for different languages and skills for your agent.

Until then, enjoy every part of this launch equally.

items.title: Reviewers rarely talk about reliability. Owners bring it up twice as often
items.author: tsxng
items.content:
Across these 14 categories: 7.8% of reviewer opinions vs17.0% of owner opinions.Owners bring it up more in 13 of the 14; tennis ball machines are the exception, with only 91 owner opinions.6,900 opinions from YouTube reviews and 3,567 from Reddit threads. Left out: video doorbells, smart thermostats, mechanical keyboards and 3D scanners, where reliability isn't a topic of its own (it's folded into a broader one such as "Connection, Reliability & Support"), and pickleball machines, which have no Reddit threads yet.

Most of what breaks shows up after the review is done

  • Search owner threads for the model plus "months" or "a year later", not just the launch reviews.
  • Check whether the device still works if the app or the company's servers go away.
  • Look at the warranty length and how owners describe getting a replacement.

Read this before the numbers

  • Reviewers aren't hiding anything. Most reviews are made in the first days or weeks with a new unit. That's too early for most failures, and it's hard to test a company's support.
  • Owners post when something goes wrong. Nobody starts a thread to say their robot vacuum still works, so these numbers show what owners worry about, not how often things break. For scale: across all topics,56% of owner opinions and 15% of reviewer opinions are negative. Reliability (70%) and apps (71%) are still well above the owners' own average.
  • If we also count mixed topics such as "Value & Support" or "Responsiveness & Key Reliability", owners bring up reliability 2.4 times as often instead of twice, and more inall 17 categories that have owner opinions. We lead with the stricter number. The same goes for apps: mixed topics like "Connectivity & Battery" are left out.
  • Some YouTube reviews are sponsored. We count them like any other source and can't reliably tell which ones are.
  • An AI model labels each opinion with a topic and as positive or negative. Every opinion links back to the sentence it came from, so any of them can be checked.
  • YouTube reviews and Reddit threads about 657 products currently on sale in19 categories, collected for BettaScore's rankings: 8,062 opinions from YouTube and 4,525 from Reddit. Review sites, forums and Hacker News (517opinions) aren't in the comparison.
  • What counts as an opinion: one source's view on one topic of one product. A source that covers five topics counts five times; a source that mentions a topic ten times counts once.
  • reliability is any topic about reliability, durability, warranty, service or support; apps is any topic about apps, software, firmware or connectivity. Mixed topics are left out of both.
  • opinions in a topic group ÷ all opinions from that platform, including neutral ones. Negative shares count positive and negative opinions only.

BettaScore ranks products by what public reviews say about them. No brand pays to be listed or to rank higher, and our shopping links earn nothing.

items.title: Four Months of Zig
items.author: ibobev
items.content:
It has been about four months since I returned to Zig after being absent for a few years. In this time, I have written some software in Zig and reengaged with the community, online and in person. I decided to share some of that experience, including what I have liked about Zig so far and what I haven't. I'll include some comparisons to Rust along the way since that was my previous go-to language.

The first project I started in Zig was snurl. It is a library for interacting with the smallnet (Gemini, Finger, Gopher, Spartan, and such). My goal has been to provide an alternative to curl for the smallnet, with similar testing and fuzzing requirements but on a smaller scale. I wanted to roughly follow TigerStyle insofar as it made sense for the project.

Something I ran into early on was that the fuzzer didn't actually work. When getting excited about fuzzing in my last post, I didn't realize that the feature had not yet been completed. This isn't surprising, considering Zig's status, but it was disappointing, especially since the fuzzer is demonstrated in the generated file provided by .

After this, I wrote a two programs which I have not published yet. The first is a small TUI typer racer. It was simpler than I expected to get a minimum version working so far. The second is an n-body simulator with stellar evolution using raylib.

The most exciting opportunity in the last few months was the chance to go to a local Zig Day. I learned of Zig Day Seattle occurring on Lobsters on August 20th. I was ecstatic to learn that there was a Zig Day in my area. Then I saw Andrew Kelley would be there and became more excited.

Zig Days are local meetups where people interested in Zig hang out, work on their projects together, and talk about Zig. For this Zig Day, I decided to work on snurl. A friend, Evin Yulo also decided to attend.

The event itself occurred in the Bothell library, moved there from the Bellevue library after so many people signed up that capacity was overwhelmed. Having the creator of Zig at the event will do that.

I love the format of these Zig Days and I'm glad they are a part of the community. Since they are run by local groups, it gives the whole Zig community a more interconnected feeling. It's a way to interact with other people who are interested in Zig in person. And, in this case, the creator of Zig itself.

I got the chance to talk with other programmers about their projects. Hopefully some ideological cross-pollination occurred that will make all our projects stronger. I ended up working on snurl with evin, who started work on integrating Zig's standard library TLS implementation as alternative backend.

I also briefly talked with Andrew Kelley. I hope Zig's built-in fuzzing gets fixed sometime soon!

I will definitely be attending Zig Day Seattle again in the future. I may even head down to Portland to catch one before the next local one comes around. I enjoy the opportunity to connect with other people interested in Zig and its values.

I love anyzig. I've had to use zig master and 0.16.0 for different projects, and anyzig has made that doable.

Unfortunately, it breaks outside of directories without a , meaning if you have tooling that requires a command to work, it can only occur in project directories. This breaks autoformatting for my one-off Zig scripts. Maybe a default zig version could be provided in that case.

I know it frustrates some people, but I love the fact that you have to pass IO and allocator parameters to functions in Zig.

I'll start with allocators, since they've been around longer. For each Zig function you have to accept an explicit allocator parameter. This is different from most programming languages which either use a default allocator that may be changed globally or one changed by a local (see Odin).

I like being able to change allocators for different parts of code. You might want an arena allocator for some things but need a general purpose allocator for others. Sometimes a is all you need to perform an operation. Zig's style makes this all obvious to handle.

I prefer Zig's system to Odin's implicit system since Zig keeps things explicit. It's clear whether a function allocates memory or not, and hard to accidentally pass in the wrong allocator.

This is also superior to Rust's hidden, infallible allocations that panic when memory is exhausted. They're working on adding explicit allocations, but this will be yet another feature tacked onto the language rather than something built from the ground up.

It's much easier to reason about programs that allocate memory in Zig.

The IO parameter is even more powerful, even if it is newer. It is well worth the breaking changes required to bring it about (even if I skipped the 0.15.0 -> 0.16.0 transition). In Zig, every function that interacts with the underlying operating system (with caveats) requires an "IO" parameter. This provides the context for input, output, and everything else. Porting Zig to new operating systems is mostly just porting IO.

Practically, this is really nice for testing. When testing behavior, you just need to put in a testing IO instance that works as you need it to. You can change the input stream however you want, cause writes to fail, and anything else.

Just like with allocation, passing an IO argument makes it clear which programs are pure and which ones are not. You can tell at a glace whether or not a program is going to modify something external.

Zig has a really good track record of keeping things simple while also adding powerful features. Instead of adding 100 small features that do slightly different similar things, it tends to provide one major feature that supports all the various other use-cases. Low floor, high ceiling.

I love comptime. It's a seamless way to do metaprogramming and precomputation all in one. Other people have written more detailed accounts so I shall move on.

Zig's build system is stellar. So much so that companies like Uber have adopted it for their software written in other languages.

One thing I like about it is that I can integrate other tools with it seamlessly in ways that Cargo complains about. This is especially important for one of my projects that involves code generation.

Zig has an excellent dependency culture. The main ethos is simple: avoid. When you don't need a dependency, don't add one. However, when you do, it's often a battle-tested library that Zig can effortlessly integrate with translate-c. You can easily also vendor in external dependencies and audit their code.

Most of my Zig programs have about one or two direct Zig dependencies, with zero indirect dependencies. This makes the codebase much easier to audit and control.

This stands in stark contrast to Rust, where the smallest of my projects regularly have a few direct and dozens of indirect dependencies.

This is thanks both to Zig's dependency culture and the fact that essential features like reflection, random number generation, clean error handling, and JSON parsing are built into the language or standard library rather than maintained as separate individual libraries. No need to depend on serde or syn in every program.

Zig encourages careful consideration before adding dependencies, and I appreciate that.

Handling Errors Effortlessly

Zig pushes programmers to handle errors correctly by default. The laziest way to handle errors in Zig is to use the keyword and add to the function's return type.

This contrasts to Rust, which leads programmers to insert panics into their code. The issue is that it's often easier to panic when prototyping, and then leave that in the code longer than it should be. I've used production code written in Rust that panic instead of returning a proper error.

In Rust you can use , which is quicker than , but you also have to do something like Result<Type, Box<dyn std::error::Error>. That's a mouthful! Alternatively, you can use the anyhow crate and return , which also provides some nice helper methods. But then you have to add a dependency for reasonable error handling. There's also Zig-style composable errors with yet another library.

The core team members at Zig have been doing amazing work at incremental compilation. If you run zig build --watch -fincremental, the compiler will watch for changes, check exactly what you changed, and then modify only what you've changed down to linking. No effort beyond what's required, so it's faster that human perception even for large codebases. Zig was designed from the ground up to support this behavior.

This makes for a really nice workflow. I can just run the compiler in incremental mode right next to my text editor, and get updates on my code as I save. No time to get distracted with something else. With Rust projects 10+ seconds incremental compilation loops were common even in smaller projects. That's enough time to get distracted but not enough time to be productive doing something else, leaving annoying gaps that Zig eliminates.

Rust is disadvantaged here. It's a stable language that needs to maintain backwards compatibility. This means it can't afford to break things in order to improve compilation speed, at least not to any large degree. Meanwhile, if it makes Zig better, the maintainers are willing to break just about anything to ensure the end result will be perfect.

Currently, Zig only supports incremental compilation on x86_64 on Linux and macOS. If you use another operating system or architecture you won't have access to this feature yet, but in that case it's another thing to look out for!

This makes Zig just a bit more wonderful to work with. I'll take it.

Like every other user of Zig, I would like to see the standard library become more stable. I know that's one of the last tasks to do before 1.0, and there are many others before then, but it is frustrating to deal with the constant breakage in the ecosystem. My understanding is that that's why 0.17.0 took so long to be released.

Andrew Kelley said at Zig Day that he would like to see 1.0 more than anyone. I believe him, so I will have patience and trust that the final version will be excellent.

This is the one reason I still use Rust for some projects. Some cases require a stable programming language and the ecosystem that provides. But considering the impressive software that's being built in Zig these days, stability isn't everything. And there are projects for which the niceties of Zig outweigh its instability. I can't wait for 1.0.

I would like to see more assistance with lifetimes in the Zig compiler. Specifically, I would like to see returning local variables to fail in debug mode, either as a kind of built-in lint (as Andrew Kelley has mentioned wanting to implement) or as literally invalidating that memory after the function returns. That way new users quickly learn to avoid that pattern. Currently, it's easy to unintentionally break your code this way, even if you think you understand lifetimes.

Relatedly, the compiler currently accepts code that will be broken in the future. The compiler lets variables live the entire scope instead of the scope of a block. This means that if you stack-allocate a buffer and return it from a block, that buffer should be invalidated but isn't. My understanding is that this could silently break in a future Zig version.

Zig is poorly documented. It has enough to get you started, but to continue onward you have to parse intention from sparse doc comments that are sometimes attached to functions. Examples are rare. I still haven't got Zig's standard library TLS working in snurl because neither I nor a friend can figure out how to set up the buffers correctly.

Because of this lack of documentation, a lot of the knowledge for building solid Zig programs is distributed across the Web. If you're well integrated into Zig communities, having read the existing documentation, watched the presentations, and read the code, you can succeed. If you aren't that well integrated, however, it can be a challenge to work effectively.

The benefit of this is that it encourages people to engage in Zig communities (I'm an admin for the Matrix room, for example). While LLMs seek to demolish human collaboration, we need human-to-human collaboration now more than ever. However, we can still have that and nice documentation too. As we all know, people will still ask questions if you have things well-documented. And a good community knows how to point people towards good resources rather than just saying "RTFM".

I would also be curious to see what the intersection of Zig and literate programming could be. My literate programming tool is written in Rust right now, but that might change.

I would love to parse JSON at compile time. For one of my projects, there is a JSON file that is stored inside the binary. It's static and could be parsed at compile time into a collection of structs.

However, the standard library JSON parser requires an allocator. Because there are no allocators that work at compile time, this means that any JSON parsing must be done at runtime. So that's what I did with my project.

I believe there is an intention of adding a JSON parser that does not require an allocator (the data already exists in the JSON string, after all). That will solve the immediate problem, but there are more general cases that may require an allocator. I believe worked at compile time before and served this purpose. It could do so again.

The one caveat to this is that it requires the compiled binary blob checked into the source code. This is better than requiring the full previous compiler (like Rust), but it's not as good as having the full source available for every step of the process at all points. A malicious actor could still sneak something into the blob. More importantly, many distributions (like Debian) cannot properly package Zig at the moment because it's impossible to do so in a way that's compliant with their guidelines.

Their original plan was to use the compiler's C backend to generate a C version of the compiler which would then be maintained separately. They would then have two different source versions. They decided this approach would be too difficult, unfortunately.

Because of this, someone will have to make another Zig compiler in another language (probably C) that will improve the bootstrap process. This is explicitly not something the Zig Software Foundation wants to develop right now. This means that at the moment there is no way to bootstrap Zig fully from source.

This issue isn't just a theoretical problem. Because Zig can't be packaged on Debian, I had to choose another language for one of my projects to ensure wider possible usage.

Fortunately, this issue is temporary. Once Zig is stable, building an alternative compiler should be straightforward. Zig is designed to be a simple language where alternative implementations are humanly achievable, unlike other languages. Currently, the instability means any alternative compiler will be playing a constant game of catch-up, which is probably why the core team doesn't want to manage it while they're rapidly iterating.

Alas, this may also require waiting for 1.0. May it come soon!

I will continue to use Zig. I'm excited about the direction it's going and I look forward to continuing to be a part of its community. So far, I've found no other programming language that I prefer more than Zig, even with its shortcomings. It's just stable enough that I don't have to make massive changes between releases. It will continue to be my go-to programming language for most projects.

One of these projects is ReTangled. It was previously written in Rust but I grew tired of the massive dependency trees and want to take full advantage of Zig's build system.

I've also been looking to contribute more to Zig directly. Between my limited time as a student, Zig's overflow of contributors already, and the poor documentation, this will be a challenge. But I want to contribute back, make an impact on the project, and become a better software engineer. Thankfully, improving contributor onboarding seems to be a priority for Andrew Kelley moving forward.

I'll also be at future Zig Days in Seattle, if you want to meet and work on Zig projects together!

items.title: Introducing LFM3: Every Modality for Specialized Intelligence
items.author: Philpax
items.content:
Today, we’re excited to announce , our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs) built for specialized intelligence. The LFM3 model family is multimodal by nature and brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one new shared backbone. The first release of the LFM3 family covers models in the 2B parameter range.

Built on a new hybrid architecture and 22T tokens of pre-training, LFM3 is far more expressive than LFM2 while maintaining its efficiency. The extra capacity in a small, fast model makes LFM3 the ideal starting point in its class for specialized intelligence: this is because it can be fine-tuned locally, it can run on any device, and it is capable enough to become a reliable expert on a specialized task.

The base and post-trained models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face, our Playground, and the Liquid AI API. Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune them locally.

New architecture for more expressivity

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention could run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. Its design came from our automated hardware-in-the-loop architecture search. For LFM3, we used this search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts.

We also expanded the hardware in the loop, from CPUs in one phone and one laptop for LFM2 to 14 device and backend combinations for LFM3: phones (Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra and OnePlus 15), a Raspberry Pi 5, laptops (Apple M4 Max and AMD Ryzen AI), and Arm and x86 cloud CPUs, plus GPUs and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

Gated short convolutions still make up over half the layers. To add capability without slowing down long contexts, we tried swapping some of them for other sequence blocks, and sliding-window attention (SWA) gave the best quality–speed tradeoff. We kept the other changes described below only where they improved quality without a meaningful speed cost. The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster.

LFM3 combines three operators: gated short convolutions, sliding-window attention (SWA), and global attention. Of its 24 layers, 13 are convolutions, 5 are SWA with a 256-token window, and 6 are global attention. The convolutions also use a kernel size of 7, up from 3 in LFM2.

Head-wise gated attention. A sigmoid gate scales each head’s output, so a head can switch off when it has nothing to add. This can help suppress activation outliers that hurt quantization and improve training stability.

Global attention layers rotate only the highest-frequency half of each head and leave the low-frequency half unrotated, so those dimensions match on content regardless of distance. SWA layers keep full RoPE.

Each block normalizes both its input and its output, which helps keep activations well-scaled.

LFM3 uses the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B, built to tokenize non-Latin scripts more efficiently.

LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens. Compared with LFM2, the mix adds more scientific papers, repository-level code, a wider range of knowledge sources, and considerably more math. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated, higher-quality data, with a larger share of agentic traces and diverse tool calls to prepare the model for agentic post-training. This stage also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

A multimodal family for every need

The first LFM3 release includes six models, all branched from the same LFM3-1.7B-Base backbone and all around 2B parameters. Four of them cover different input modalities (text, vision, audio, and omni), and the last two are decision models specialized from the vision and omni models. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you can pick the one that fits your use case, customize it, and run it on-device.

For a deeper dive into the performance and inference results behind these models, refer to the respective model cards.

is a text model for local agents and specialized applications with a 256K-token context window.

It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It can triage your inbox, manage your calendar, research topics on the web, send you morning briefings on WhatsApp, and use tool search to find the right tool among thousands of options. Since tokens are free, dozens of agents can run continuously in the background. You can adapt it to your domains, harnesses, and tools with a short fine-tuning run on a single GPU.

On agentic tasks, LFM3-1.7B competes with models several times its size. It leads on instruction following and function calling on BFCL and ToolSandbox, and beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps (WebArena-Verified, AutomationBench). Larger models still win on agentic coding and knowledge, where size matters most, but search helps close the knowledge gap, nearly doubling its score on Humanity's Last Exam.

To achieve these results, the model went through four stages of post-training:

  • Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): 1.75T tokens across various tasks, including chat, reasoning, tool calling, and agentic traces.
  • Mixed reinforcement learning: many domains trained at once, from math and code to SQL and structured outputs. A length penalty in the reward keeps answers concise.
  • Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD): six specialist RL teachers (code, math, tool use, long context, agentic work, and enterprise workflows) are distilled back into a single model.
  • tasks from web browsing to office work are run inside real agent harnesses, preparing the model for deployment.

On-device, we measure metrics with llama.cpp at Q4_0 and a 32K-token context. LFM3-1.7B is the fastest model on all three devices, decoding 1.8 to 2.8 times faster than the next one, and it uses the least memory. Long contexts stay cheap: a full 128K-token context needs 1.6 GB of KV cache, against 4.3 GB for Qwen3.5-4B and 5.6 GB for MiniCPM5-2B.

On a single NVIDIA B300 with SGLang in BF16, LFM3-1.7B can produce 3.6 billion tokens per day at 1,024 concurrent requests, more than any other model in this comparison.

To show what this throughput makes possible, we ran more than 300,000 LFM3-1.7B agents in parallel to investigate the Enron email archive.

LFM3-1.7B can be served at low latency under random traffic, enabling real-time use cases like online fraud detection when run on . P95 request latency remains stable even under heavy load, outperforming competing models served on vLLM.

LFM3-VL-2B can watch, reason, and understand the physical world:

  • for the first time, an LFM vision model takes video as input. Ask questions about a recorded lecture, a walkthrough filmed on your phone, or a clip from a camera feed.
  • the model reasons step by step before answering. This helps it better understand user inputs and solve harder visual questions such as math, charts, and multi-step problems.
  • Spatial and embodied reasoning: the model’s ability to localize objects and reason about their spatial relationships provides a strong foundation for downstream robotics applications.

LFM3-VL-2B is a leap in performance over the LFM2.5-VL series. Across 62 vision benchmarks, LFM3-VL-2B scores significantly ahead of all models of similar size by at least 7.4 points, and despite its size, it matches the performance of Gemma 4 12B, a model more than 6 times larger, surpasses Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite and is within 2 points of GPT-5.6 Luna. For more details, see the model card.

Notes: Each category score is the unweighted mean of its benchmark scores. The Average row is the unweighted mean across all 62 evaluations.

All of this can be run efficiently on-device, which enables everyday use of intelligence without the data leaving your device or the need for a cloud connection. On-device, LFM3-VL-2B has the highest prefill throughput and lowest memory footprint across all measured devices, compared to other models of its size class.

On a single NVIDIA B300 with SGLang in BF16, LFM3-VL-2B can produce over 12,000 tokens per second, higher than any other model of the same size class.

LFM3-VL-2B can be served at low latency under random traffic, enabling real-time use cases like image asset tagging when run on . P95 request latency remains stable even under heavy load, outperforming competing models served on vLLM.

In addition to improvements to the LFM3 backbone, LFM3-VL comes with our new in-house vision encoder which uses 3× less compute than the SigLIP2 encoder in previous LFM VL models.

The Liquid vision encoder combines convolution and attention to make it significantly more efficient than its ViT counterpart at the same quality. The performance-efficiency graph below illustrates this. Our 164M-parameter encoder matches Qwen3.5-2B’s vision encoder at 55.9% average accuracy across 13 vision-language model benchmarks, while requiring 2.2× fewer FLOPs. 

For video, the encoder jointly embeds each pair of sampled frames into one temporal slice of visual features, halving the temporal sequence length before further encoding. Together, these choices make the encoder a foundation for both richer image understanding and efficient video processing.

LFM3-Audio-2B is a compact, fully featured audio model that runs locally on laptops and edge devices. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both.

LFM3-Audio-2B uses a new architecture with an audio encoder and codec developed in-house. It outperforms LFM2.5-Audio in speech quality and now supports 18 languages. New capabilities include audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling.

  • ask questions aloud and receive streaming replies in text and speech. For text-only responses, the model can also reason before answering.
  • transcribe, synthesize, and translate speech across 18 languages.
  • Audio understanding and reasoning: ask the model to interpret recordings and answer questions about the speech, sounds, and events they contain.
  • turn spoken requests into tool calls to control apps and devices. The model can also respond in text or speech alongside those calls.

ASR (WER, %, lower is better)

English TTS (UTMOSv2, 1-5, higher is better) (WER, %, lower is better)

VoiceBench, Tool calling, Audio understanding (audio in, text out, %, higher is better)

Our new LFM-based audio encoder is built from a mixture of sliding-window attention and short-convolution layers, keeping memory utilization bounded. The new encoder is fully causal, allowing the model to process live microphone input and perform prefill while you speak. This reduces the wait after you finish, with time to the first token as low as 50 ms.

LiquidCodec, our new audio tokenizer, powers multilingual speech generation in both LFM3-Audio and LFM3-Omni. Built on the LFM3 architecture, LiquidCodec turns generated tokens into speech at about 87× real time on a single CPU thread (Apple M4 Max), supporting streaming decoding. 

Quantization compresses each 80 ms of speech into 12 discrete tokens and, in contrast to previous LFM Audio models, allows multiple tokens to be predicted iteratively in parallel rather than requiring sequential prediction. As the backbone generates new tokens, the detokenizer progressively converts them into speech, all faster than real-time so that conversations are smooth and responsive.

LFM3-Omni-2B is our first omni model, bringing vision, audio, and language together in a single model that can see, listen, and talk back:

  • Spoken visual question answering: Ask questions about images or real-world scenes using speech, and receive answers in text, speech, or both.
  • Audio-visual video understanding: Process video frames alongside their corresponding audio, allowing the model to reason about both what is happening on screen and what is being said or heard.
  • Combine visual context with spoken instructions to generate structured tool calls, enabling assistants to interact with applications and interfaces using both what they see and what users say.

LFM3-Omni supports cross-modal interactions that require understanding visual and auditory information together. Users can ask spoken questions about images, or provide videos with synchronized audio and ask questions that depend on both what is seen and what is heard.

In addition to cross-modal understanding, LFM3-Omni retains the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and language instruction following.

LFM3-Omni-2B is designed for efficient deployment in resource-constrained environments. Its capabilities enable conversational assistants that can provide context-aware guidance, support hands-free interactions, and help users complete tasks through natural voice commands. By combining visual understanding, spoken dialogue, and tool calling, it can support applications ranging from personalized education and everyday assistance to navigation of digital interfaces and robotic systems.

At 2.2B parameters, it brings this kind of multimodal assistant on-device. Examples include a tutor that looks at your handwritten math and answers your spoken question, a tablet you can walk around with and ask about what it sees, and in-car assistants that combine what the camera sees with what the driver says.

This release also brings two new decision models: d1-2B, built on LFM3-VL-2B, reads text and pictures, and d1-Omni-2B, built on LFM3-Omni-2B, also listens. Instead of writing an answer, they decide in milliseconds. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability.

Beyond the new LFM3 backbone, the big change since d1-3B is . On top of yes/no, choices, and scores, both models can now:

  • draw a box around what you describe, or find every instance of something, with a count.
  • pull text, numbers, and dates out of a document, with the exact span they came from, and say “not found” when a field isn’t there.
  • give a number with its likely range.
  • select every option that applies, each with its own probability.

Ask as many questions as you like: they’re read in one pass over the same input.

d1-2B replaces our previous d1-3B, with a third fewer parameters:

d1-Omni-2B takes the same questions over audio, so a voice request can be routed, checked, or answered just like a typed one. Asked by voice instead of in writing, it keeps nearly all of its accuracy:

It also recognizes everyday sounds (84.5% on ESC-50) and tells which of 43 languages is being spoken (92.5% on FLEURS).

Pick d1-2B for text and pictures, and d1-Omni-2B when your inputs include audio. Both run on-device, and turn a stream of tickets, documents, calls, or camera frames into structured decisions without a round trip to the cloud.

In the following demo, d1-2B runs on a MacBook. You describe what to find in plain language, and it draws a bounding box around every match in a single forward pass, using the new Point answer type.

Made for specialized intelligence

LFM3 is built to be specialized. The 2B-class models are small enough to fine-tune on your own data and run where your application lives. The following two examples show this with LFM3-VL-2B. The first is a short fine-tune that turns it into an inspection model for one narrow industrial task. The second is a research extension that turns it into a robot controller.

Domain expertise: Specializing LFM3 for your field

While frontier models are powerful generalists, they are not necessarily experts in your particular use case. In this demo, we fine-tuned LFM3-VL-2B to find and classify defects in drone photos of wind turbine blades. Training used about 3,000 public photos () with SFT and GRPO for a few hours on one A100. We then compared it with the base model and GPT-6 Luna on about 1,400 held-out photos.

Out of the box, LFM3-VL-2B and GPT-6 Luna correctly identify these defect types in fewer than 10% of images. A short fine-tune raises LFM3-VL-2B’s classification accuracy to 67% and improves detection F1 from 0.003 to 0.11, compared with 0.01 for GPT-6 Luna. Lightning-strike images illustrate the difference, where GPT-6 Luna often locates the defect correctly but labels it incorrectly, while the fine-tuned model correctly identifies a lightning strike. Beyond classification and detection, the model can answer natural-language questions about the same image. For example, it can locate visible damage or write a brief inspection finding including the defect type, supporting evidence, and location.

Robotics: teaching LFM3 to act

We investigate how LFM3-VL-2B can serve as a basis for robotics applications. We consider three complementary directions: (1) high-level tool orchestration, (2) vision-language navigation, and (3) low-level manipulation.

Building on LLM-based robot planning and control (SayCan, Code as Policies) and recent physical orchestrators (VoLo, Gemini Robotics ER 2), we fine-tuned LFM3-VL-2B to operate a robot arm through tools. Given a request and the current camera image, it reasons step by step, grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, and manipulates them via motion planners. It then checks each outcome in the next image and reports back, including when a request is out of reach or ambiguous. The tasks feature relational selection, sorting by measured properties, and environment perturbations, all simulated in Isaac Sim. No architectural change was needed. A rank-32 LoRA adapter was trained on about 40,000 samples, combining manipulation trajectories with general tool-use and pointing data, and took about six GPU-hours on a single AMD Instinct MI325X. Paired with a fine-tuned d1-2B skill monitor, we can further double recovery success under disturbances such as slips, jams and drags.

For vision-and-language navigation, LFM3-VL-2B reads a route description and a short history of RGB frames to predict navigation targets and residual-quantized trajectory primitives, inspired by the action interface of LightNav-0. Each decision consists of five tokens: two spatial/control tokens and three hierarchically quantized codes encoding a ten-waypoint path that a velocity controller can track. We only repurpose 2,068 vocabulary tokens; the architecture is otherwise unchanged. We train on 2.8 million samples for 72 GPU-hours on MI325X GPUs. In unseen validation scenes, the resulting model achieves success rates of 53% on R2R and 43% on RxR under a strict continuous-control evaluation protocol with wall sliding disabled and explicit stopping required. We further observe robustness across varying camera angles and instruction languages. On a Jetson AGX Orin, our navigation model updates waypoint trajectories at over 2.5 Hz using TensorRT FP16 without visual prompt caching.

To turn LFM3-VL-2B into a vision-language-action (VLA) model, we adopt parallel action prediction inspired by OpenVLA-OFT and StarVLA-α: a small residual MLP maps the hidden states of eight action-query tokens to an eight-step chunk of continuous robot actions in a single forward pass. Proprioception is provided both as discretized text and through an embodiment-specific learned projection, and the whole network is fine-tuned end to end. We trained a single generalist checkpoint for 170 GPU-hours on MI325X GPUs, on simulated and real-robot data from 15 embodiments, ranging from single arms and mobile manipulators to bimanual platforms and a humanoid. The resulting VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks. On a Jetson AGX Orin, it can generate action chunks in under 50 ms using TensorRT at FP16 precision.

Start building today with LFM3, available on and the .

With LFM3, we're delivering on our vision of AI that runs anywhere. These models are:

  • download, fine-tune, and deploy.
  • native support for llama.cpp, MLX, and vLLM across Apple, AMD, NVIDIA, SGLang and Qualcomm hardware. Deploy on for low-latency, high-volume workloads.
  • from base models for customization to specialized text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models, one architecture covers diverse use cases.

We can't wait to see what you build.

We are grateful to our day-0 launch partners for their support. LFM3 is ready to use today across these platforms: Ambarella, AMD, Arm, Intel via OpenVINO, NVIDIA, OpenRouter, Qualcomm via Qualcomm AI Hub and GenieX, and Vercel. Thanks to Mercedes-Benz and Shopify for partnering on pre-release testing and evaluation.

Thank you to our builder ecosystem for its support: Atomic, Cactus, Hugging Face, llama.cpp, LM Studio, MLX, Ollama, RadixArk on SGLang, .txt, Unsloth, vLLM, and ZML.

items.title: Classification of Finite Simple Groups Formalized in Lean
items.author: pfdietz
items.content:
The classification of finite simple groups is one of the great collective achievements of mathematics. Its first-generation proof spans thousands of journal pages, written by about a hundred mathematicians over several decades. It shows that every finite simple group is cyclic of prime order, alternating, of Lie type, or one of 26 sporadic groups.

Here we present a complete formalization in Lean following the first-generation proof, with every logical step checked by Lean’s kernel. Along the way, we found an issue in a published argument for the Unbalanced Group Theorem. The accompanying paper explains the issue and the alternative route used in our proof. Our blog post tells the full story.

items.title: Why Micron Is Suddenly Ditching 4F² DRAM as Rivals Double Down
items.author: rbanffy
items.content:
DRAM is fundamentally different from logic. Logic cells are like those in your processor, and in that form, they're all the same sort of thing: switching transistors. DRAM is different because each cell is made up of a transistor and a capacitor, and that complicates scaling. For a long time now, we've been making those cells with a geometry known as "6F²", and the 'holy grail' was the ultimate move to 4F², offering a theoretical 33% density improvement. Now, Micron says that despite putting "over two decades" of research into the technology, it's shifting gears and sticking to 6F² for the foreseeable future.

This might seem odd, but you have to understand that these are cell geometries, not process nodes. In essence, these terms describe the shape and layout of the DRAM cell, not its physical size directly; that is determined by the combination of layout and process node. DRAM doesn't use the same node nomenclature as logic; because of the mixed cell type (transistors and capacitors), it doesn't scale the same way; to mark node changes, DRAM vendors

currently use terminology like "1γ" and "1δ"—those being the Greek letters gamma and delta, used in this case to signify linear improvements over time. Micron's ultimate decision not to bring 4F² memory products to market is fascinating in the context that all three of its competitors, those being Samsung, SK hynix, and CXMT, are moving ahead with 4F² designs, with CXMT in particular claiming it will have 4F² RAM in server DDR5 RDIMMs by the end of the year. Conversly, Micron held a webinar on Wednesday that announced its future roadmap, above, and talked about a variety of upcoming products, not just this decision to skip 4F². That's arguably the most surprising news, though.

Scott DeBoer, Micron's President and CTO, says DRAM density is ultimately set by the spacing required by the capacitors, not by the nominal cell footprint. While shrinking the geometry from 6F² to 4F² seems like an easy win on paper, according to DeBoer, it doesn't actually gain you much in terms of density, and it drastically

increases cost and complexity. He noted that Micron "invented" 4F² and that the firm has been trying to figure out how to commercialize the technology for "over two decades," before finally scrapping it. What is Micron doing instead, then? Well, it's aggressively scaling 6F² DRAM, for one thing. The firm's roadmap notes that high-density 1δ (1-delta) memory is ramping yields, 1-ε (1-epsilon) featuring advanced wafer bonding is in development, and looking ahead to the future, it sees "ζÅ" (zeta-Angstrom) and "ηÅ" (eta-Angstrom) as its future for planar DRAM. But the real future, according to Micron, will be in 3D DRAM. Rather than simply stacking DRAM on top of logic—this is the "wafer bonding" Micron mentioned—3D DRAM describes memory devices where multiple physical layers of DRAM storage cells are stacked vertically on top of each other.

Flash memory has been doing the 3D thing

for more than a decade, of course, but flash memory relies on simple charge-trap transistors that can be stacked like floors in a skyscraper. DRAM cells, by contrast, are dynamic; each bit requires a delicate, high-aspect-ratio capacitor paired with a transistor that inevitably leaks charge. Flipping those tall capacitors sideways and scaling them vertically without thermal crosstalk or signal destruction requires a total overhaul of the basic DRAM architecture. That transition won't happen overnight, but as 2D scaling hits its absolute physical limit, 3D DRAM is where the industry is inevitably headed.In the short term, Micron could face challenges if its competitors are able to economically manufacture 4F² memory at scale. Regardless, the company is placing a massive strategic wager that 4F² will prove to be a costly, short-lived detour. If Samsung, SK hynix, or CXMT end up burning billions in capital expenditure to adopt vertical-channel transistors only to hit an early brick wall with capacitor scaling, Micron will look brilliant for skipping the headache. By wringing every last drop of efficiency out of established 6F² lithography with High-NA EUV, advanced materials, and wafer-on-wafer bonding through the zeta and eta eras, Micron hopes to preserve its cash and engineering bandwidth for the real prize: being first to cross the finish line when true monolithic 3D DRAM finally becomes economically viable.
