items.title: Fixing Tool-Call Accuracy in vLLM
items.author: coffeemug
items.content:
For a tool-call to succeed, the call must adhere to the tool’s schema.

The simple approach to tool calling is to let the model generate tool calls freely and trust that the model’s training is sufficient to generate correct calls. This is similar to how we trust the model to generate syntactically correct prose.

The simple approach works most of the time because modern models are good at following structured patterns. But success “most of the time” implies that many tool calls can still fail, resulting in context window pollution due to error messages, lower model performance, and increased cost due to the agent having to retry the call one or more times.

To avoid such experiences when using Kimi, Moonshot AI published their K2VV ToolCall benchmark. This benchmark lets providers verify that they serve Kimi with the same quality as the original, including its default behavior of only generating valid tool calls.

K2VV ToolCall’s workload consists of 2000 requests selected to evaluate when the LLM generates tool calls and whether the generated tool calls are syntactically correct (i.e., adhere to the provided schema). The benchmark allows analyzing the model’s quality by quantifying two metrics:

and . Trigger similarity considers when the service decides to trigger a tool call, and how similar its decisions are to Moonshot AI’s own service. Schema accuracy quantifies the fraction of tool-calls that adhere to the tool’s schema and can therefore be invoked successfully. For example, when tool-call accuracy is 50%, half of the tool calls generated by the model are malformed.

Schema accuracy usually falls short due to the probabilistic nature of language models. A model generates tokens based on likelihood. It is not running a compiler or type checker. Even with a clear prompt, it can still produce malformed tool calls. This can be caused by, for example, a mismatch between the model’s training data and the current inference harness. Models are trained on many tool-calling datasets, each with its own tools, schemas, and conventions. As a result, a model may generate a tool or field name that it has seen during the training, even if it does not exist in the current production environment. For example, it may generate

when the available tool is , or use when the active schema expects .

items.title: SS United States to be sunk as largest artificial reef
items.author: geox
items.content:
The SS , once the fastest passenger liner in the world, is scheduled to be sunk in the Gulf of Mexico in November, creating what will be the world’s largest artificial reef.

Officials from Okaloosa County, Florida, have confirmed that the 302m (990ft) ship will be scuttled approximately 22 nautical miles (25 miles; 41 km) southwest of Destin-Fort Walton Beach.

The sinking has been scheduled for the second week of November, although the exact date is dependent on weather conditions.

Built in 1951, the SS was designed to serve as both a luxury passenger vessel and military transport if so required.

She was awarded the Blue Riband for the fastest transatlantic crossing of 3 days, 10 hours, 40 minutes on her maiden voyage in July 1952, beating the record set by Britain’s RMS 14 years earlier by 10 hours and two minutes.

The rise of commercial air travel eventually brought her ocean-going career to an end in 1969, after the ship’s operating costs began to overrun her income.

Despite several offers to buy her and a plan by the US Navy to turn her into a hospital ship, she remained laid up in Norfolk, Virginia until 1992.

She was subsequently towed to Sevastopol Shipyard in Ukraine to have her asbestos linings removed, but despite changing hands several times since then, she was eventually returned to the US and spent almost three decades slowly deteriorating at a mooring in Philadelphia.

In 2011, she was bought by the SS Conservancy, a consortium of business owners who planned to redevelop the ship as a luxury waterfront development.

Disagreements over rent with the owners of the pier where she was docked led to a legal battle, which ended with the ship being ordered to vacate her mooring in September 2024.

Shortly before the eviction, officials from Florida’s Okaloosa County announced that they were involved in negotiations to acquire the ship and sink her as an artificial reef, at an estimated cost to the County of $1 million.

The ship finally departed Philadelphia in February 2025, arriving in Mobile, Alabama, the following month, where contractors began the extensive process of stripping and cleaning the vessel in preparation for her sinking.

According to a recent progress report by Okaloosa County, work to remove hazardous materials from the ship is now complete, and a renewal of the county’s existing permit to create artificial reefs has been authorised by the US Army Corps of Engineers, removing a major regulatory hurdle to the sinking.

All 128 fuel and lubricant tanks have been emptied, cleaned and certified safe by a marine chemist, and more than 200 samples have been collected to assess potentially hazardous materials, including polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).

Remediation and inspections across all 12 of the ship’s decks have been completed; exterior paint and deck coverings found to contain high concentrations of PCBs have been removed.

The ship’s distinctive red, white and blue funnels have also been removed, together with her radar mast and propellers, hundreds of fittings and more than 400 portholes.

Many of these artefacts will be preserved and displayed in a land-based museum being planned to celebrate the ship’s history.

The county has also completed seabed surveys of the proposed deployment site, using multibeam and side-scan sonar to identify obstacles and ensure that existing natural and historical features will not be damaged.

A digital model of the entire ship has been produced to preserve a record of her condition before sinking.

According to the latest update, will be sunk by controlled flooding rather than explosives, with the intention that she settles upright on the seabed.

Openings have been prepared to enable access for marine life and divers, while compartments considered to be unsafe have been sealed.

The ship is expected to rest in approximately 55m (180ft) of water, with her upper decks reaching depths of around 17–18m (55–60ft), making the wreck suitable for recreational and technical divers alike.

At 302m long, she will surpass the aircraft carrier USS , sunk off Pensacola in 2006, as the largest vessel deliberately sunk to create an artificial reef.

Okaloosa County says the project will provide new habitat for marine life while creating a major attraction for the region’s diving and fishing industries. Researchers from several US marine science institutions are also expected to monitor the wreck’s environmental impact after deployment.

The SS United States Conservancy says further details of the sinking operation, including arrangements for a public livestream, will be announced once the final deployment date has been confirmed.

items.title: SIMD-accelerated computer vision on a $2 microcontroller
items.author: zdw
items.content:
I wrote an accelerated FAST feature detector for the ESP32-S3 that leverages its 128-bit SIMD instructions. It achieves roughly double the performance of the reference implementation, and takes around ~6ms to process a QVGA (320x240) frame. You can find the source code here.

For its price, the ESP32-S3 is a powerhouse of a microcontroller. Within its unassuming plastic package lies a dual-core CPU running at a maximum of 240MHz with a slew of peripherals, including WiFi and Bluetooth Low Energy radios. While digging through its technical reference manual I discovered that the chip supports a limited set of SIMD instructions. For silicon that’s cheaper than the average coffee, that’s pretty cool. Let’s see what exciting things we can do with it!

In the process of writing a SIMD-accelerated FAST corner detector, I learned the basics of assembly on the ESP32-S3, worked around its eccentric limitations, and ended up writing my own basic register allocator, .

After some more web browsing, I realized that these instructions weren’t exactly secret, but rather relatively unknown. I wanted to experiment with them myself and write more advanced code than what I could find online. As I’ve been really interested in computer vision lately, I decided on writing a SIMD-accelerated implementation of the FAST feature detector for the ESP32-S3.

I started by looking for example code that uses SIMD instructions. At the time of writing, I could only find three sources:

After perusing through them, I was relieved to find that assembly on the ESP32-S3 isn’t that bad. I settled on this general structure:

From there, I started writing a SIMD-accelerated version of the FAST corner pre-test. Essentially, it samples one pixel in each cardinal direction and checks if there are at least three “extreme” pixels. In this case, an extreme pixel is one whose absolute difference from the center pixel is above a certain threshold.

I decided on a function that would calculate the extrema count of sixteen pixels at a time, since each vector register can store sixteen eight-bit values. This would be achieved by sampling four “chunks” of pixels in each cardinal direction and comparing them to their respective center pixels.

However, this is where I ran into my first limitation- the ISA doesn’t allow for direct misaligned reads. Under the assumption that the center pixel would be aligned, the east and west blocks would be misaligned:

Thankfully, the chip has an that allows for extracting a slice of two concatenated registers into another one. Using this functionality, I was able to extract the east and west blocks by reading and extracting slices from the two blocks adjacent to the center block.

Okay, so now I have the pixel data. Time to do some comparisons, right? Wrong. Turns out the ESP32-S3’s only implements comparisons for signed eight-bit numbers. This made processing a little more difficult, because all my pixel data was stored as unsigned eight-bit numbers. If you just reinterpreted the unsigned data as signed data, you get some weird results:

The range gets nonlinearly mapped to , breaking all compare operations. To make this work, I needed to shift the range of the values from to . This should’ve been a simple subtraction, but the instruction set got in the way again: on the ESP32-S3, all the SIMD arithmetic operations are saturating, which meant that all pixel values above 127 would end up being clamped at -128 instead of underflowing to their appropriate values. To overcome this problem, I had to somehow subtract 128 from each number in parallel without using the subtraction instruction. This seemed like a daunting task to me at first, but I eventually arrived at a solution.

Let’s assume that is the . Here is its digits’ place values:

Notice anything interesting? Subtraction is the same as addition by -128, so to compute , we can just “increment” the number by -128 by adding one to ’s most significant digit, whose place value is -128. We can compute this by simply flipping the highest bit of . Since XORing any bit with one is the same as taking the bitwise NOT, we can selectively flip the highest bit of by XORing it with the bit mask , which equal to . Therefore, .

Now, whenever unsigned eight-bit values are loaded in, they are XOR’d with to convert them an appropriate (linear) range where the arithmetic and comparisons make sense again.

With those two tricks, I was able to circumvent the limitations of the ESP32-S3 and write the SIMD-accelerated FAST corner pre-test. I also wrote a SIMD-accelerated scoring function using a similar set of operations but I won’t be writing about that here.

In the end, I was able to improve the throughput of the FAST feature detector by about 220%, from 5.1MP/s to 11.2MP/s in my testing. This is well within the acceptable range of performance for realtime computer vision tasks, enabling the ESP32-S3 to easily process a 30fps VGA stream. Not bad for $2!

items.title: Neural chip decodes interactions between brain regions
items.author: giuliomagnifico
items.content:
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) is a therapeutic technique that delivers electrical pulses to specific areas of the brain via an implant to modulate neural activity. It is already widely used for movement disorders such as Parkinson’s disease, and researchers are increasingly exploring its potential for severe psychiatric illnesses including major depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder.

However, most existing DBS systems operate in what engineers call an “open loop” manner: stimulation is delivered according to predefined settings rather than continuously adapting to the patient’s brain activity. Even among closed-loop, or adaptive systems, many rely on signals recorded from a single brain region. This is a major limitation for psychiatric disorders, where clinically relevant information may be distributed across networks of interacting brain regions.

“Our work is based on the growing body of research suggesting that psychiatric disorders arise more from disruptions in communication between brain regions than from dysfunction of any single region,” explains Mahsa Shoaran, head of the Integrated Neurotechnologies Lab in EPFL’s School of Engineering and Neuro-X Institute.

Shoaran and her team have developed a low-power, implantable neural system-on-chip. Dubbed LogSync, it records brain activity and extracts biomarkers that describe the strength of brain waves (oscillations) and synchrony between signals from different brain regions. A machine-learning algorithm then analyzes these network-level biomarkers to distinguish cognitive and emotional states, and generate stimulation triggers when specific states are detected.

The work, published in the IEEE Journal of Solid-State Circuits was developed as part of a CHF 6.6 million grant from the US National Institute for Mental health (NIMH) to develop implantable systems capable of measuring and controlling oscillatory brain networks for severe psychiatric illnesses, particularly mood and anxiety disorders. It builds on the lab's previous work on brain-to-text decoding and closed-loop neuromodulation, extending these concepts to network-level biomarkers and adaptive decoding for future psychiatric therapies.

More targeted stimulation at lower power

The researchers evaluated LogSync using human brain recordings from previous psychiatric experiments. One dataset captured changes in cognitive engagement while performing a mental task, while another captured emotional arousal as participants viewed video clips. The algorithm distinguished these cognitive and emotional states from the neural recordings alone. In further experiments conducted in rats at the University of Minnesota, the implant tracked ongoing oscillations and generated stimulation triggers at predefined phases of brain activity.

Shoaran says that major challenge was achieving all this functionality while working within the very limited power budget of an implantable system.

“Our entire system is co-designed, meaning the algorithms and hardware are developed together with the constraints of implant in mind. This approach helped us achieve network-level neural signal processing and decoding on a single chip, while keeping power consumption under 200 microwatts — a fraction of that typically required by many implantable neural-interface systems,” she says. Another innovation is LogSync’s use of logarithmic computations, which simplify the complex operations needed for brain-network analysis and real-time biomarker extraction and decoding.

LogSync's initial validation focused on psychiatric applications. But the capability to extract brain-network biomarkers to trigger precisely timed stimulation is broadly applicable across next-generation neurotechnology, including adaptive DBS for movement disorders, closed-loop non-invasive stimulation, and emerging focused-ultrasound interfaces.

In parallel, the laboratory is developing new machine-learning methods that learn directly from neural recordings rather than predefined biomarkers. Their recent ICML 2026 work, which uses self-supervised learning to capture neural activity across regions, channels, and time, supports broader efforts to bring intelligent neural interfaces closer to clinical applications, including through Infera Neuro, an EPFL spin-off co-founded by Shoaran.

items.title: Air Purifiers as White Noise Machines
items.author: luu
items.content:
classic approach is a fan in a box, though in the past ten years people have mostly switched over to electronic ones. But a fan is really a great approach; you just need to put it to better use: have the fan clean the air.

Instead of spinning a fan in free air to make noise, you can have it pull air through a filter. A small purifier sounds a lot like a classic noise machine, is only a bit larger and more expensive, and removes smoke and infectious particles from the air. For example, here's a $47 purifier with a 6.5" diameter, cleaning 34 cubic feet of air per minute ("CADR") at 45dB. For most circumstances where someone would use a white noise machine, this kind of small purifier is all-around better.

Now, 34 CFM is not very much air cleaning. I usually run an AirFanta 3Pro and it cleans ~6x more air for the same amount of noise, or ~12x more air with much more noise (~56dB). On the other hand it's more expensive ($165) and bulkier (12.6" square), and arguably uglier.

Still, even a 34 CFM purifier helps a lot with smoke. If you have a 10ft square room with an 8ft ceiling and a reasonably typical 0.5 air changes per hour through leakage from outdoors, this small purifier will cut particulate levels to 16% of the outdoor level. In AQI terms (not linear) this is like going from AQI 200 to 72 or AQI 100 to 31.

items.title: Diamond Transistor
items.author: Gravityloss
items.content:
When the surface of a single-crystal diamond wafer is terminated with an atomic layer of hydrogen, its electron affinity becomes negative, allowing electrons to transfer from the diamond valence band to suitable acceptor species (often adsorbates or engineered surface layers) at the surface.

This charge transfer leaves behind a high-density two-dimensional hole gas (2DHG) confined within a few nanometers of the surface, producing p-type conductivity while preserving the intrinsic purity, thermal conductivity, and breakdown strength of the diamond bulk.

Because no ion implantation or lattice substitution is required, surface transfer doping avoids defect generation and carrier scattering associated with conventional doping, making it particularly attractive for high-power, high-frequency, and radiation-hard electronic device platforms.

items.title: Overgrown, when plants invade your abandoned tabs
items.author: speckx
items.content:
I was doing a little creative exercise the other day around the word "Overgrowth". The first thing that came to mind was an apocalyptic scene, something like The Walking Dead or The Last of Us, where plants tend to overgrow abandoned buildings.

I then wanted to apply this idea to the digital world, and the word "abandoned" made me think of my browser tabs... What if my tabs were slowly taken over by plants the longer I left them unread? What if I had to clear away these invasive plants to access my tabs again? A bit like trying to open a door that's been overgrown...

So I built this fun little Chrome extension that does just that. It won't necessarily make me read my tabs more but it's ok.

  • Every tab has a neglect clock. It runs while the tab is out of view and stops while you're looking at it.
  • The longer a tab is neglected, the more plants grow over it, from the edges towards the middle.
  • Once a tab is more than 5% overgrown, the page behind the vines is walled off: you can scroll, but you can't click, select or drag anything.
  • To free it, you have to slash through the vines by dragging your mouse across them. Get it down to 5% and the last bits fall off. If you abandon your tab once more, the jungle starts growing again.
  • Just for fun, you can pick your weapon of choice between the rusty machete, the chainsaw and the flamethrower.
  • You can also change how long it takes for your tabs to be fully overgrown.

Originally, I was thinking about blocking users from closing their overgrown tabs until they slash all plants, but I thought it would be too annoying... 😅

The code is organised in 3 main parts: the background logic, the content script to display the plants and animation on the tabs and the popup folder that handles the UI of the extension itself.

The background.js file starts the jungle on each open tab and forgets it when it closes.

This folder handles the UI for the extension with some small components for the time setting, the weapon choice, the list of tabs and their current stat.

The folder contains the SVGs for the plants and the weapons, the logic to position and grow the clusters, the and the sounds.

I've been wanting to get back into building things for a while now and this project felt like a small, fun way to start. I'm writing this on a new computer so I currently "only" have 22 tabs open but 14 of them are already completely overgrown... 😂 It might not make me read them more but slashing through the vines makes coming back to them more fun! 🪚🌿

items.title: Faster than earcut: triangulating 3.7M map polygons in 489 ms
items.author: molind
items.content:
We have published the polygon triangulator of our map engine as a small library, earstrip, under the ISC license, the same one earcut uses. It is one C++ header, and a WebAssembly build on npm that takes the same arguments as earcut. In C++ it is 14% faster than earcut.hpp, in the browser 1.4 to 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js, and the comparison is near the end. This post is about how we got there.

A GPU fills triangles and nothing else. A map, on the other hand, is mostly polygons: buildings, parks, parking lots, the strip of grass between two tram tracks. Here are a few blocks of Śródmieście in Warsaw the way our renderer reads them from a map file, :

Before any of this gets a fill, every outline has to be cut into . Hover over a polygon, or tap it, to see what it turns into. These blocks hold 331 polygons with 5,151 vertices, and they become 4,514 triangles.

Zoom level 13 of our offline map of the Masovian Voivodeship, the region around Warsaw, has 3,740,425 polygons. On one core of an M4 Pro, the constrained Delaunay triangulator in our engine needs 2.93 seconds to cut all of them. This October I replaced it with ear clipping. To write this post I rebuilt the ear clipper one idea at a time, one commit per idea, and timed every commit on those same 3.7 million polygons, so each section below ends with a number.

A triangulation of a set of points is Delaunay when no point lies inside the circle through the three corners of any triangle. Two triangles that share an edge are enough to see how the rule works. Drag the point D:

While D stays outside the dashed circle through A, B and C, the shared edge is AC. and the edge flips to BD; and it flips back. Each flip is a local repair, and a triangulation where no edge wants to flip is Delaunay. Of all the ways to triangulate the same points, it has the largest smallest angle. The arc marks the smallest angle of the two triangles, and the line under the figure shows what the other diagonal would give: wherever you put D, the edge the circle rule picks wins.

"Constrained" means that the polygon's own edges must stay edges of the triangulation, even where the circle rule would flip them away. Our triangulator inserts the vertices one at a time. For each new point it walks across the triangles built so far until it finds the one the point falls into, splits it, and flips edges around the new point until the circle rule holds again. It also forces the polygon's edges in, and at the end it keeps only the triangles that lie inside the polygon and outside its holes.

Well-shaped triangles matter when you interpolate something across them or run a simulation on them. A flat fill doesn't care: a GPU fills a needle-thin triangle as correctly as a fat one. And most of the work is spent on polygons that hardly need any. Almost half of the Masovian polygons, 1.8 million, have four vertices or fewer. A triangle needs no cutting at all and a convex quad is two triangles, yet the Delaunay code spends 302 ms on them, building each triangulation from scratch.

An ear of a polygon is a corner you can cut off with one straight cut. Take three consecutive vertices a, b and c. If the corner at b is convex and no other part of the polygon reaches into the triangle abc, that triangle is an ear. Cut it off, and what remains is a polygon with one vertex fewer. In 1975 Gary Meisters proved that every simple polygon with more than three vertices has at least two ears that don't overlap. So there is always another ear to cut, and a polygon with n vertices falls apart into n − 2 triangles.

Here is one of the buildings from the blocks above. Move the slider to cut its ears one at a time, or :

The triangle is the next ear to go. The algorithm needs one test, "is this corner an ear?", and the simplest version of it checks the corner and then every other vertex of the boundary. is the 2×2 determinant found in every geometry codebase; it is positive when c lies to the left of the line from a to b, so for a boundary that runs counter-clockwise a positive means a convex corner:

A point on an edge of the triangle counts as inside: if the ear touched the rest of the boundary, cutting it off would leave a polygon that touches itself. The one exception is a point at exactly the position of a, b or c, which happens where an outline meets itself at a single vertex. Holes make that common.

Ear clipping works on one closed boundary, and 11,345 of the Masovian polygons have holes, such as courtyards and clearings in forests. The way to deal with them is to cut each hole open and stitch it to the outer ring with a bridge, an edge from a vertex of the hole to a vertex of the boundary, walked once in each direction. The boundary then runs around the outside, crosses the bridge, goes around the hole the other way and comes back. There is no area between the two copies of the bridge, so the polygon is the same, but now it is one ring.

The bridge must not cross anything. David Eberly's write-up of ear clipping has a neat way to find one. Take the rightmost vertex of the hole, m, and cast a ray to the right. The first edge the ray hits, at I, has an end P further to the right. If no boundary vertex lies inside the triangle m, I, P, the bridge m–P is safe. You can drag the hole around:

the triangle is empty and the bridge goes to P. the sits inside the triangle, and the bridge goes to the dent instead: of the dents in the triangle, Eberly takes the one closest in angle to the ray. Holes are bridged rightmost first, so a hole further left can bridge to one that is already part of the boundary.

Map data adds two cases of its own. Our coordinates are integers on a tile grid, so a ray along a grid line runs all the time; the crossing test passes over such a vertex, and my first version got exactly this case wrong. And mappers often draw a courtyard that at one point. Such a hole needs no bridge: the two rings are joined at the shared vertex.

The naive clipper (−1,812 ms)​

With holes bridged, the first complete version walks around the boundary, tests corners with the above, cuts every ear it finds and writes each triangle as three indices. On the Masovian polygons it takes 1.12 seconds, 2.6 times faster than Delaunay. The chart splits each time by polygon size; hover over a part of a bar to see its number, or click a row:

is shorter than in every size class but the last. The 1,123 largest polygons, with 257 vertices or more, take 199 ms to clip and 90 ms with Delaunay. Each ear test there walks hundreds of vertices, and a polygon needs hundreds of tests, so the cost grows with the square of its size. The rest of this post is about making the ear test cheaper and needed less often.

Test only the dents (−237 ms)​

Look at which vertices can actually stop a convex corner from being an ear. Say some vertices lie inside its triangle, and take the one closest to the corner itself. Its two edges can't cross the sides of the triangle, so both run back, away from the corner, and the polygon wraps around that vertex from the corner's side. That makes it a reflex vertex, a . So if anything is inside the triangle, a dent is inside it too, and the test only has to look at the dents.

The engine keeps a list of them. A dent leaves the list when cutting its neighbour makes it convex, and a convex corner never turns into a dent, so the list only shrinks. The test becomes:

The 28.1 million ear tests now look at 185 million points instead of 353 million, and the total drops to . That is less than you might expect, because building outlines have a lot of dents. The building with the arch above has 15 of them among its 27 vertices. And the smallest polygons get slower, from 34 to 54 ms: for a triangle or a quad, sorting the corners into dents and the rest costs more than the walk it saves.

Skip tests on convex polygons (−2 ms)​

A polygon without dents is convex, and every corner of a convex polygon is an ear, so it can be cut without a single test. Checking for that needs care. "Every corner turns left" is not enough:

The turns left at all five corners, because it goes around its centre twice. The engine adds one more condition. Walking around a convex ring, the edges go right along the bottom and left along the top, so their x direction changes exactly twice, at the leftmost and the rightmost point. The passes; the star changes direction four times, at the corners, and goes to the ordinary ear tests. Both counts come out of the same loop that marks the dents, so the check costs almost nothing. Triangles and quads get their own shortcut before that loop.

The shortcut removes 4.4 million of the 28.1 million ear tests, but those were the cheapest ones: a ring without dents has nothing to scan. On its own it barely moves the total, , though the polygons with four vertices or fewer win back part of what the dents cost them, from 54 to 48 ms. It matters more in the next step, where a convex ring becomes a single strip.

So far every triangle costs three indices. A GPU can also draw a triangle strip, where each new index adds a triangle made of it and the two before. A convex ring makes one strip if you zig-zag across it:

The ear clipper can write strips too. Cutting an ear makes the corners of its two neighbours sharper, so they are good candidates for the next ear, and cutting one of them extends the strip by a single index. The engine tries them first and keeps alternating between the two ends while the ears last. In its code the neighbours of the cut vertex are a and b:

When the next corner is not an ear, the strip ends and the walk goes on from where it stopped. The 21.5 million triangles now take 35.8 million indices instead of 64.5 million. The ear tests don't get fewer: the naive walk already went on at the next corner after a cut, and now every strip also ends on a test that fails, 25.0 million instead of 23.7 million. Still, the total falls to , and the largest polygons drop from 146 to 103 ms.

Sort the dents into buckets (−65 ms)​

A forest or a lake can have thousands of vertices and hundreds of dents, and each ear test still reads every one of them. When a polygon has more than 32 dents, the engine sorts them into buckets along the longer side of their bounding box, about two dents per bucket. An ear test looks only at the buckets that its triangle spans. As dents turn convex and leave, the index is rebuilt once half of it is gone.

Points scanned fall from 181 million to 101 million, almost all of it on the large polygons: the polygons with 257 vertices or more go from 103 to 57 ms. Total: .

Count without branches (−178 ms)​

The loop in the dent test exits at the first dent inside the triangle. Most of the time there is none: the test reads all the dents and says yes. An early exit then buys nothing, and the three comparisons per point are branches the CPU has to predict. The engine first runs a pass that only counts dents inside the triangle, with no branches at all:

The smallest of the three determinants is non-negative exactly when the point is inside the closed triangle. Only when the count is not zero does the exact loop from before run, to rule out dents that sit on a corner. The bucket version does the same with a bounding-box test, 64 points at a time into a bit mask. The total falls to , and the middle sizes gain the most: polygons with 33 to 256 vertices go from 327 to 216 ms.

Test only the marked dents (−30 ms)​

When the count is not zero, the exact loop reads all the dents again, although the first pass has already seen which ones were inside. The bucket version keeps that in its bit mask. The short list, up to 32 dents, can do the same: the first pass sets one bit per hit instead of counting, and the exact test looks only at those dents:

Points read fall from 128 million to 120 million. This is the last step, and it is the code of earstrip as published: , 6.0 times less than Delaunay on the same polygons.

Meisters' theorem is about simple polygons. Map data is rounded to a tile grid, and rounding can break a simple polygon. Here is the outline of Warszawa Śródmieście, a railway station less than a kilometre from the blocks above, rounded to grids of different size. The orange rings mark vertices that land on the same point as their neighbour:

per tile side, the grid our map files use, a grid step is 18 cm. Even there 31 of the 154 vertices merge with a neighbour, because mappers often place points a few centimetres apart, and the outline survives. nearly half of the vertices merge, and the clipper still cuts it. the rounded outline touches itself in a way that leaves no ear at all, and at 10 bits it happens to work again.

When the clipper walks all the way around the boundary without finding an ear, it drops the corners that have no area and walks once more. If that fails too, it gives up, and the engine triangulates that polygon with the Delaunay code, which still exists for this. In the Masovian data 76 polygons end up there. They come from a map built before the last change on the other end: our map generator now rounds every polygon to the final grid with GEOS's snap rounding and checks that ear clipping can cut it. In a fresh build of the Masovian map that repaired 273 polygons, and ear clipping can cut every polygon in the file.

Delaunay has one more job. Every hole needs its own bridge, and finding one scans the whole boundary, so a polygon with thousands of holes pays for thousands of scans. Our world map has a polygon with 11,675 holes: ear clipping takes 606 ms on it, Delaunay 17 ms. The engine now sends every polygon with 128 holes or more to Delaunay. In the Masovian data that is two polygons.

The library keeps both of these fallbacks inside. earstrip covers a polygon with a constrained Delaunay triangulation of its ring edges when the ears run out, when the triangles they leave cover the wrong area, and when it has more than 128 rings; in C++ and in JavaScript say which way a polygon went. On the 56,472 polygons of our world map tiles, with up to 11,675 holes in one, earstrip takes 459 ms and earcut.hpp 2,892 ms. On the zoom 13 polygons that the ears can't cut exactly, earcut's triangles differ from an even-odd fill of the rings on 31% of the pixels on average, earstrip's on 0.15%.

Before the new clipper went into the app, I compared it with earcut, the ear clipper behind MapLibre and Mapbox GL, in its C++ version earcut.hpp 3.2.4. Natively the two are close, and that could have been the end of it. But we are working on a web renderer that runs the same C++ engine compiled to WebAssembly, so I went further and compared the browser side too: both clippers compiled to WebAssembly, and earcut.js 3.2.4, the JavaScript original that web maps run today. For that I took the clipper out of the engine into earstrip. On all 5.8 million polygons of our test sets it writes exactly the engine's strips, and its repository has these polygons and the code behind every number in this section. Its native benchmark is the one behind the chart above, and the native row below is the last step run against earcut.hpp. Every WebAssembly build gives exactly the same triangles as its native version on all 4.4 million polygons of zoom levels 13 and 9. Milliseconds for the 3.74 million polygons of zoom 13, best of 7, one thread, V8 in Node and JavaScriptCore in Bun:

WebAssembly, loop inside the module, V8 / JSC
WebAssembly, one call from JS per polygon, V8 / JSC
npm package, one call per polygon, V8 / JSC
npm package, direct calls, all polygons in one call, V8 / JSC

Natively earcut.hpp is 14% slower than earstrip. Compiled to WebAssembly and run in V8, earstrip loses 23% and earcut.hpp loses 67%, almost all of it in its main loop that searches for ears. It isn't the allocator: builds with mimalloc and emmalloc give the same time. I haven't dug further. In V8, earcut.hpp in WebAssembly ends up only 19% faster than plain earcut.js, and 10% once each polygon is a separate call from JavaScript.

The package rows are what a web page gets, and the earcut column there is earcut.js. The call that replaces earcut takes the coordinates as JavaScript numbers and returns a new array of triangle indices every time: 1.4 times as fast as earcut.js in V8 and 1.6 times in JavaScriptCore. About half of what it loses against the loop inside the module goes into copying the coordinates in and turning the strips into a list, the rest into calling into WebAssembly once per polygon. The direct calls skip all of that: the polygons go straight into the module's memory and come back as one index buffer of strips for WebGL 2 or WebGPU, 1.7 and 2.1 times as fast as earcut.js.

Some of the ideas above are in earcut too. It also relies on the fact that only a dent can block an ear, but it checks that last, for every vertex that passes the bounding box and triangle tests, instead of keeping a list of dents. Above 80 vertices it links them in z-order and scans only the stretch of that curve the triangle's bounding box covers, which does the job of the buckets. What it doesn't have are the shortcut for convex polygons, the strips and the count without branches: it writes three indices per triangle and stops at the first point inside.

earstrip is on GitHub and npm, with the polygons from this post and the code to time it against earcut on your own machine.
